title: In 1858, a 98-word telegram across the Atlantic took 16 hours
body: The first transatlantic telegraph cable was laid in August 1858 by two converted warships, HMS Agamemnon and USS Niagara, between Valentia Island in Ireland and Trinity Bay in Newfoundland. New York fired a hundred-gun salute, but the signal was so faint and slow that Queen Victoria’s **98-word** greeting to President Buchanan took 16 hours to send. The cable’s electrician, Wildman Whitehouse, tried to force messages through with up to 2,000 volts, which wrecked the insulation; after three weeks and 732 messages the line fell silent. The successful 1866 cable managed 8 words a minute.

slides.label: to transmit Queen Victoria’s 98-word message in August 1858
slides.text: The 1866 cable, laid by the giant Great Eastern, managed about 8 words a minute, roughly 80 times faster.

slides.heading: Telegraph speed across the Atlantic, in words a minute
slides.note: 98 words in 16 hours works out at about a tenth of a word a minute; the 1866 cable managed 8

events.text: Agamemnon lands the cable at Valentia

slides.heading: What killed it
slides.text: Signals crawled through the long cable because of an effect William Thomson called retardation; he argued for a thicker cable and gentle currents, and clashed repeatedly with the cable’s electrician, Wildman Whitehouse, whose attempts to drive up to 2,000 volts through the line broke down its insulation within weeks.

slides.question: Why did the 1858 cable die after three weeks?
options: The company ran out of money
slides.explanation: Wildman Whitehouse’s repeated attempts to drive up to 2,000 volts through the cable compromised its insulation, and in September 1858 it failed altogether.

slides.heading: Which is not a cable ship?
slides.explanation: Trinity Bay is the Newfoundland landing point of the 1858 cable. Agamemnon and Niagara laid that cable, and the Great Eastern laid the successful one in 1866.
